newsitem.title: USA: Final game to decide man vs computer chess match.
newsitem.headline: Final game to decide man vs computer chess match.

text.p: World chess champion Garry Kasparov will strive to put aside his fear of supercomputer Deep Blue on Sunday in a clash that will decide the outcome of their exciting re-match.

After five games over eight days, the man and the machine are tied going into the sixth and final game, the improved and modified Deep Blue having shaken the confidence of the player considered to be the best in the history of the ancient game.

"I have to be afraid because I can outcalculate any player in the world easily but I cannot outcalculate this machine," Kasparov said after Saturday's fifth game, in which the IBM system forced him into agreeing to a draw following some artful endgame strategy.

Deep Blue is an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess that can examine hundreds of millions of possible moves per second. Since their first match in Philadelphia in 1996, the machine's speed has been doubled and it has been infused with more chess knowledge. Kasparov won the Philadelphia match.

Kasparov, 34, and Deep Blue, a play on IBM's nickname Big Blue, have won one game each and drawn three consecutive games for a match score of 2-1/2 points each. One point is awarded for a win and a 1/2 point for a draw.

Sunday's game was scheduled to start at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT) with the computer playing with the white pieces and the advantage of the first move. The match winner will receive $700,000 and the loser $400,000.
"It's an important game, but it's probably more important for the outside world than it is for me," the Russian grandmaster said.

The event is part chess match and part research project to help build computers that can make complex, simultaneous calculations for applications such as weather forecasting, air traffic control and molecular dynamics, according to IBM.
"As the match progresses every game is better than the previous one," said Deep Blue team manager Chung-Jen "CJ" Tan. "I'm sure the game will be the best of the six-game series."

Kasparov easily won the first game on May 3, but then the system played brilliantly in the second game, the turning point psychologically and emotionally for the champion. In an oversight rarely seen in grandmaster play and never before from Kasparov, he needlessly resigned in a drawn position.

The error was confirmed in post-game analysis and Kasparov said it affected his performance in the next two games, both draws. But Deep Blue deserved the draw on Saturday when it fought the endgame in a manner that won admiration from expert observers.
